scenes.narration: Every computer stores negative numbers the same way: two's complement. Here's how it works.
captions: Every computer stores negative numbers the same way.

scenes.narration: Look at the leftmost bit. It is called the most significant bit. If it is zero, the number is positive. If it is one, the number is negative.
captions: The leftmost bit is the most significant bit.

scenes.narration: Take plus five. In four bits, that is zero one zero one. The leading zero is the sign, and it says positive.
captions: Sign bit 0 — this number is positive

scenes.narration: To negate it, flip every single bit. Zeros become ones, and ones become zeros. This is the one's complement.
Now add one. One zero one zero plus one is one zero one one. That is minus five.
And it checks out. Plus five plus minus five is one zero zero zero zero. The extra bit falls off, and we are left with zero.
captions: The carry out of the sign bit is discarded
Every number plus its complement is zero

scenes.narration: That is why four bits reach from minus eight up to plus seven. One more negative value than positive, because zero needs a home.
captions: Four bits hold sixteen values: −8 to +7
Zero counts once — so negatives get one extra

scenes.narration: Flip the bits, then add one. That is two's complement.
